title: Whose swan?
told: a later telling of the Buddha’s life

hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? have you ever found a hurt animal, and had to decide what to do?
options: then you and this boy have something in common. listen.
I didn’t know what to do
that happens. listen to what he did.
then picture it with me. listen.

steps.line: Here’s a much-loved later telling. Young Siddhattha was walking in the palace gardens when a flock of swans flew overhead.
steps.label: a later telling

steps.line: His cousin Devadatta drew his bow and shot. One swan tumbled from the sky, an arrow in its wing, and came down near the prince.
Siddhattha got there first. He knelt, gently drew out the arrow, and held the bird close to calm it.

steps.q: Devadatta runs up. “That’s my swan. I shot it.” What happens next?
o: They take it to the wise men of the court
The two boys fight over it
steps.why: Neither boy would give in, so the grown-ups had to decide.

steps.line: So they took it to the wise men of the court. “I brought it down,” said Devadatta. “I kept it alive,” said Siddhattha.

steps.q: How do you think the court decides?
o: It belongs to the one who saved it
It belongs to the one who shot it
steps.why: Saving a life counted for more than taking it.

steps.line: The court said: a life belongs to the one who saves it, not the one who tries to take it. The prince nursed the swan, then let it fly.

steps.q: The prince won the swan. Why does he let it fly away?
o: It was too badly hurt to keep
Saving it was never about owning it
The court ordered him to set it free
steps.why: He wins the case, then gives up the prize. Protecting a life and then letting it go is kindness without grabbing.

steps.pre: The first of the five precepts, kept across Buddhist schools, is to refrain from
steps.why: Not harming life comes first. Lying is the fourth precept, and while many Buddhists choose not to eat meat, many others do.

steps.q: Devadatta comes back later in the Buddha’s life. As what?
o: His most loyal monk to the very end
The king who gave him a monastery
His jealous rival inside the order
steps.why: In the old texts Devadatta becomes a monk, then tries to take over the order and even to kill the Buddha. This later telling plants him early.

steps.line: Today, a kid carries a stunned bird to a shoebox lined with soft towels. Small hands, the same choice.
steps.label: today

say: to be honest about this one: it isn’t in the oldest buddhist texts. it’s a later telling, made famous in english by a long poem of 1879, and told to children ever since.

the teaching under it is old, though. the first of the five precepts, shared by every buddhist school, is to refrain from taking life. the dhammapada gives the reason: every being fears harm, so put yourself in their place. it’s week three’s metta, with gentle hands.

steps.q: Week three began with metta, wishing every being well. What does the swan story add to it?
o: Metta is a feeling you keep to yourself
Metta means always siding with the weaker one
Metta reaches even a bird, and moves the hands
steps.why: Every being, the Metta Sutta says. Wishing well becomes kneeling down and drawing out the arrow.

today.say: today, notice one small life near you: a plant, a pet, an insect at the window. tend it the way the boy did, slowly, with gentle hands. if you like, let a little metta go its way.
options: gentle hands. that’s the whole lesson.

card.keepWhy: A life belongs to who protects it.
sources: Edwin Arnold, The Light of Asia (1879), Book the First: the swan shot by Devadatta, the prince drawing out the arrow, the dispute before the sages, “the saver of a life” owns it
Earlier versions of the swan episode in Sanskrit and Chinese lives of the Buddha (e.g. the Abhiniskramana Sutra, Chinese Fo benxing ji jing, T190)
The first of the five precepts (panatipata veramani)
Dhammapada 129–130: all tremble at the rod; putting oneself in the place of others, one should not kill or cause to kill
